title.script: Welcome, everyone! Tonight isn't just a tour of three fancy algorithms — it's a bake-off, and here's your one-sentence cheat sheet for each contestant. KNN compares, asking "who are my nearest neighbors?" SVM separates, drawing the cleanest possible dividing line. And the neural network learns, building its own representations from scratch. Here's the twist though: there's no automatic champion — the winner depends entirely on the data in front of you, and by the end you'll be able to explain exactly why.

story-no-champion.script: Here's a story with no permanent champion. For a while, nearest-neighbour methods ruled by simply remembering examples. Then support-vector machines took over many tricky problems by drawing one disciplined boundary, and in 2012 a deep neural network transformed image recognition by learning its own features. But here's the twist: none of the older methods ever became wrong — they still win on the right data. So on a real project, the honest move isn't reaching for the fanciest model; it's testing sensible options fairly and letting the data decide.

concept-three-minds.script: Here's a neat way to think about three different machine learning models. Give them all the exact same data, and each one makes a different bet about what really matters. K-nearest neighbors trusts the examples sitting closest to you, saying "you're probably like your neighbors." An SVM instead hunts for the widest, safest boundary between the classes. And a neural network takes a bolder approach, learning its own intermediate features that make the groups easier to tell apart.

concept-knn.script: Here's one of the simplest ideas in machine learning: to classify a new point, just look at the examples nearest to it and let them vote. Training does almost nothing, but every prediction means measuring distance to all your data, which gets expensive. Now watch what happens with our mystery point. Its single closest neighbour is a pedestrian, so k equals one says pedestrian, but widen the circle to three or seven and signs win the vote. That number k is really a dial that controls how local or how smooth your decisions are.

quiz-knn-k.script: Here's a really interesting situation. Your model gets every single training example right, but the moment one noisy point sneaks in, its predictions go haywire. Does that pattern sound familiar? It should — remember last class, that deep decision tree that memorized everything and then fell apart? Different model, same symptom: it's memorizing, not learning. So the smart move is to try a larger odd value of k and check it on data the model hasn't seen, letting validation tell you how much smoothing this dataset can actually handle.

concept-scaling.script: Here's something sneaky about KNN that trips up a lot of people. When it measures distance between points, it listens loudest to whatever feature has the biggest numbers. If one feature ranges from one to ten and another from zero to one, that first one totally dominates, even though it isn't more important. Watch what happens here: the exact same query's nearest neighbor flips from sign to car after we standardize. No labels changed, only the ruler we used to measure. And always fit your scaler on training data only, then reuse it, or you'll leak information.

concept-svm.script: Imagine all of you are data points scattered across this room, and I need to draw a line that separates two groups. Now, lots of lines would do the job — but the support-vector machine is picky. It wants the widest possible aisle, the biggest empty corridor between the two sides. The students standing right at the edge of that aisle? They're the support vectors, and they alone decide where the line goes. Move someone in the back row and nothing changes, but nudge a support vector and the whole boundary shifts.

quiz-svm-margin.script: Here's a quick geometry check for you. Imagine you grab one training point that's sitting way out, far from the margin, and you slide it around while all the support vectors stay put. What happens to the decision boundary? The key insight is that support vectors are the ones anchoring everything — they're literally what the machine is named for. So moving a faraway point usually does nothing, while nudging a point right on the edge is what actually shifts things.

concept-kernel.script: So here's the beautiful second trick of support vector machines. Sometimes no straight line can separate your data — picture two interlocking crescent moons, there's just no flat cut that works. A linear kernel gives you that one flat boundary, fast and easy to interpret, but it fails on the moons. The RBF kernel instead measures how similar points are to certain landmarks, which lets it draw a smooth curved boundary. Just remember: the settings C and gamma both control flexibility, and you tune those on validation data, never on your final test set.

concept-first-nn.script: Alright, let's build our very first neural network. Picture it as three layers: we feed in the 64 pixel values from an 8-by-8 image of a digit, those flow into 32 hidden units that learn useful combinations like strokes and loops, and finally we get 10 scores, one for each possible digit. Now, each unit takes a weighted sum of its inputs, adds a little bias, and then applies a non-linear twist. That twist is the secret ingredient, because without it, stacking layers would just collapse back into a single boring straight-line model.

And once you scale that up to 32 neurons in a layer, you're suddenly training over two thousand numbers. See how fast this grows?

concept-nn-learning.script: Here's the beautiful thing: the network learns through the very same loop we saw before, just at a much bigger scale. Pixels flow forward and become ten scores, we measure how wrong those scores are, then backpropagation works out exactly how much each weight contributed to the error, and finally we nudge every weight a little downhill. What do we gain? Flexible, curved boundaries and features the network discovers on its own. But it costs us more parameters, more tuning, harder interpretation, and usually a lot more data.

quiz-fair-pipeline.script: Here's a subtle but important question about keeping your model comparison honest. Look closely at that first tempting option: if you scale the entire dataset before splitting, your scaler has already peeked at the test data's distribution. That's leakage, even if it only nudges your score a tiny bit. The clean approach is one shared split where each model gets a pipeline whose scaler learns only from the training rows. Scientific discipline is built from exactly these small, honest choices.

Think about it: with a tiny dataset where you need to explain every prediction, KNN pointing to nearest neighbors is beautiful, but it pays a heavy price at prediction time. Millions of raw images? That's neural network territory, but only if you have the compute to feed it. So pick one deployment and defend your choice using data size, speed, interpretability, and boundary shape — not because it's trendy.
